sop.text:
I am applying to the PhD program in Computer Science at Cornell to work on multilingual natural language processing—specifically making large language models useful for the hundreds of millions of people who speak Indian languages but are poorly served by today's systems.

My starting point was a concrete failure. In 2025 I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences and found that two open 7B models lost 18–26 points compared with monolingual Tamil inputs [lib:cv]. People in Chennai do not address a chatbot in monolingual Tamil; they switch registers mid-sentence. That gap became my first-author workshop paper—"Code-Switch Robustness of Open LLMs for Tamil–English," published at the Student Research Workshop of an ACL-family conference in 2026 [lib:cv]—and convinced me that evaluation design, not just training data, is a central bottleneck in multilingual NLP [lib:interests].

At Microsoft Research India in summer 2026, mentored by Dr. Anjali Mehra, I worked on the adaptation side of the same problem [lib:cv]. Extending a SentencePiece vocabulary with 6,000 Kannada-specific tokens cut average token count per sentence by 41% and improved downstream QA F1 by 3.4 points at an identical fine-tuning budget [lib:cv]. The lesson was that targeted, low-cost changes to the tokenizer can matter as much as expensive continued pretraining—relevant for any language where unlabeled text is scarce [lib:interests].

A Spring 2026 course project extended this into the speech domain: I trained a small wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio and reached 31% WER on a held-out test set [lib:cv]. Many Indian languages have far more spoken data than written data, and I want to understand how speech-text pipelines can reduce dependence on curated text corpora [lib:interests].

These three threads—parameter- and data-efficient LLM adaptation, evaluation methodology for code-switching and cultural grounding, and speech-text models for low-resource languages—define the research agenda I want to pursue in a PhD [lib:interests]. My secondary interests in retrieval-augmented generation for health and government information and in model compression for on-device inference connect directly to deployment realities in India, where network connectivity and device capability vary widely [lib:interests].

I bring a CGPA of 9.21/10 (top 5% of my department) from NIT Tiruchirappalli, a peer-reviewed first-author publication, and hands-on experience with the full stack from tokenization through fine-tuning and evaluation [lib:cv] [lib:profile]. As a teaching assistant for a 120-student Introduction to Machine Learning course in Fall 2026, I have practiced explaining technical material clearly [lib:cv]. Organizing my department's NLP reading group—now about 25 members—has given me practice in identifying which papers shift a subfield's assumptions and which are incremental [lib:cv].

Cornell's PhD program is where I want to do this work. I am excited about the program's research in natural language processing and its environment for rigorous, systems-minded empirical work. I am applying for the Fall 2027 intake and intend to identify specific faculty whose current projects align with multilingual evaluation and efficient adaptation as I develop my application.

The core question I want to answer over five years is tractable: given a new Indian language, a modest amount of unlabeled text, and a fixed compute budget, what combination of tokenizer design, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and evaluation protocol yields a model that is actually useful to a native speaker—including when that speaker code-switches? Answering it requires combining insights from NLP, speech processing, and human evaluation, which is why a research-focused PhD program is the right place to pursue it.
